write.desc: This topic defines the derivative as a limit of difference quotients, separates differentiability from continuity with examples, and proves the differentiation rules (sum, product, quotient, chain, inverse) with full proofs. Its points belong together because each rule is proved from the definition and the earlier rules, as in a single textbook section.

points.name: The derivative at a point
points.what: The learner can state the definition of f'(c) as the limit of (f(x) - f(c))/(x - c) as x tends to c, and the equivalent form with (f(c + h) - f(c))/h, explain why the two forms agree, and read the derivative as the slope of the tangent line and the best linear approximation f(c) + f'(c)(x - c).
outside: epsilon-delta definition of the limit of a function at a point

points.name: Computing derivatives from the definition
points.what: The learner can prove from the definition, using epsilon-delta arguments or the limit laws, that constants, x, x^2, 1/x and sqrt(x) have their expected derivatives, writing each proof out in full.
outside: algebraic limit laws for limits of functions

points.name: One-sided derivatives and the derivative on an interval
points.what: The learner can define left and right derivatives, knows that f'(c) exists exactly when both exist and agree, and understands the derivative as a function on an interval, using one-sided derivatives at closed endpoints.
outside: one-sided limits of functions

points.name: Differentiability implies continuity
points.what: The learner can prove that if f is differentiable at c then f is continuous at c, by writing f(x) - f(c) as the difference quotient times (x - c) and taking limits.
outside: definition of continuity at a point
algebraic limit laws for limits of functions

points.name: Continuous but not differentiable
points.what: The learner can show that the converse of 'differentiable implies continuous' fails: |x| at 0 (one-sided derivatives differ), x^(1/3) at 0 (difference quotient tends to infinity, a vertical tangent) and x sin(1/x) at 0 (continuous, but the difference quotient sin(1/x) has no limit), and knows that Weierstrass built a continuous function differentiable nowhere.
outside: squeeze theorem for limits of functions
sequential criterion for limits of functions, used to show a limit does not exist

points.name: Sum and constant multiple rules
points.what: The learner can prove that (f + g)' = f' + g' and (kf)' = kf' at a point where f and g are differentiable, so differentiation is linear.
outside: algebraic limit laws for limits of functions

points.name: The product rule
points.what: The learner can prove (fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c) by adding and subtracting f(c)g(x) in the difference quotient, and can point to where continuity of g at c is used.
outside: algebraic limit laws for limits of functions

points.name: The power rule by induction
points.what: The learner can prove (x^n)' = n x^(n-1) for every positive integer n by induction using the product rule, and hence differentiate any polynomial.
outside: proof by mathematical induction

points.name: The reciprocal and quotient rules
points.what: The learner can prove (1/g)'(c) = -g'(c)/g(c)^2 when g(c) is nonzero, explaining why g stays nonzero near c, then derive the quotient rule from it and the product rule, and extend the power rule to negative integer exponents.
outside: a function continuous at c with nonzero value at c is nonzero on a neighbourhood of c

points.name: The chain rule and the gap in the naive proof
points.what: The learner can state the chain rule (f o g)'(c) = f'(g(c)) g'(c) and explain exactly why the tempting proof that multiplies and divides by g(x) - g(c) fails: g(x) can equal g(c) for x arbitrarily close to c, as for a constant g or g(x) = x^2 sin(1/x).
outside: composition of functions and limits of composite functions

points.name: Caratheodory's form of differentiability
points.what: The learner can prove that f is differentiable at c exactly when there is a function phi, continuous at c, with f(x) - f(c) = phi(x)(x - c) for all x, and then phi(c) = f'(c); they can use this form to reprove that differentiability implies continuity.
outside: definition of continuity at a point

points.name: A correct proof of the chain rule
points.what: The learner can write a complete proof of the chain rule using Caratheodory's form, composing the two factorisations so that no division by g(x) - g(c) is ever needed.
outside: composition of functions continuous at the right points is continuous
algebraic limit laws for limits of functions

points.name: The derivative of an inverse function
points.what: The learner can prove that if f is continuous and strictly monotone on an interval and differentiable at c with f'(c) nonzero, then the inverse is differentiable at d = f(c) with derivative 1/f'(c), and can explain why the inverse is not differentiable at d when f'(c) = 0 (as x^3 at 0).
outside: the inverse of a continuous strictly monotone function on an interval is continuous
sequential criterion for limits of functions

points.name: Derivatives of n-th roots and rational powers
points.what: The learner can use the inverse function theorem to prove (x^(1/n))' = (1/n) x^(1/n - 1) for x > 0, then the chain and power rules to differentiate x^(m/n), and can relate the failure at 0 to the vertical tangent of x^(1/3).
outside: existence of n-th roots of positive reals

points.name: x^2 sin(1/x): a derivative that is not continuous
points.what: The learner can show that f(x) = x^2 sin(1/x) with f(0) = 0 is differentiable everywhere, computing f'(0) = 0 from the definition with a squeeze argument and f'(x) = 2x sin(1/x) - cos(1/x) elsewhere with the rules, and prove that f' has no limit at 0, so a derivative need not be continuous.
outside: squeeze theorem for limits of functions
sequential criterion for limits of functions, used to show a limit does not exist
derivatives of sin and cos (familiar values, used without proof)
